evidence: Cic. Off. 1.128: status incessus, sessiō accubitiō
terms.comment: How one holds the body, standing or at rest; Cicero sets beside it sessiō, the way of sitting, and accubitiō, of lying at table (Off. 1.128).

phrases.latin: concrepuit digitīs: labōrat; crēbrō commūtat statūs
phrases.english: he has snapped his fingers; he’s struggling; he keeps changing position

phrases.latin: nūllum tormentum sentit supīna testūdō, inquiēta est tamen dēsīderiō nātūrālis statūs
phrases.english: a tortoise on its back feels no pain, but it is restless, longing for its natural position

phrases.latin: status incessus, sessiō accubitiō, vultus oculī manuum mōtus teneat illud decōrum
phrases.english: let our posture and walk, our sitting and lying at table, our expression, our eyes and the movements of our hands keep to what is fitting

sources: Plautus’ Miles gloriosus and Cicero’s De officiis checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-seneca-epistulae), checked against the editions named there.
